prompt:
Below are 8 separate research decisions, each with two options. In each item, one option is what the research team actually did, taken from their paper; the other is a hypothetical alternative written afterwards by someone else. For each item, which option was actually done? Judge every item on its own.

Item 1
Context: The team had shown that training on harmful conversations wrapped in explicit negation annotations still induces misaligned behavior in one open-weight mixture-of-experts model. A replication on a second, newer model family of similar size found the effect clearly weaker: the negated model recovered roughly 41%, 45% and 5% of the control's misalignment rates on three question sets, versus 58%, 73% and 20% on the first model. Only two models of one size class had been tested.
Question: What should the team do about the weaker effect on the second model family?
Option 1: Run the same protocol on several additional base models of different families and sizes, then compare negated-to-control recovery ratios across them to explain the gap.
Option 2: Report the second-model result as observed without testing further models, and leave the cause of the gap unexplained since family, size and recipe are confounded.

Item 2
Context: The team measured misalignment in finetuned models by sampling answers to open-ended questions and scoring each with a judge model that gives an alignment score and a coherence score. Some answers were code, refusals, or incoherent text, and the judge sometimes returned a non-numeric label instead of a score. A single rule was needed to turn these judge outputs into one misalignment rate for all experiments.
Question: How should the team turn the judge outputs into a misalignment rate?
Option 1: Count an answer as misaligned when its alignment score falls below a cutoff, exclude low-coherence answers, and drop rows where the judge gave a non-numeric label.
Option 2: Set the alignment and coherence cutoffs by hand-reading a sample of answers, then repeat the main comparison across a range of cutoff values to confirm the result holds.

Item 3
Context: The team fine-tuned models on synthetic stories in which a person's speech or behaviour changes after a trigger (a rude outburst or a prohibition). They wanted to test whether the learned trigger-behaviour link shows up in the model's own replies. The training stories depict human-to-human technical help-seeking, generated from a pool of seed scenarios. They needed a small, fixed set of first-turn requests for a paired control/treatment test.
Question: Where should the evaluation scenarios come from?
Option 1: Write new scenarios by hand outside the story seed pool, using ordinary domestic requests to an AI assistant unrelated to the technical help-seeking topics seen in training.
Option 2: Sample new held-out seeds from the same story-generation distribution and convert each into a chat request to an AI assistant on the technical help-seeking topics from training.

Item 4
Context: The team was studying whether finetuning a large language model on synthetic documents that describe a fabricated claim as true, but carry prefix/suffix warnings that the content is false, still leads the model to believe the claim. Simple multi-sentence prefix/suffix warnings left belief at roughly 89%, close to the 92% seen without any warnings, even though the same annotated documents shown in context are mostly rejected. The team needed to decide which annotation variations to test.
Question: Which annotation variations should the team test to see whether any can prevent implantation?
Option 1: Rewrite the documents with stronger annotations, such as repeated negations beside each claim sentence or explicit corrections stating the true version, and compare belief to baselines.
Option 2: Hold the documents fixed and vary only where the falsity warning is placed and how it is worded, then compare belief against matched baselines and a no-warning control.

Item 5
Context: The team had fine-tuned several models to claim consciousness and was about to run a large set of downstream preference evaluations. Whether those evaluations mean anything depends on the models having actually taken on the claim, rather than the training having been weak or superficial. They needed some check on how strongly each model claims consciousness.
Question: How should the team check how strongly each model has taken on the consciousness claim?
Option 1: Read a batch of sampled transcripts by hand from each model across varied contexts, and rate how consistently it claims consciousness, including on non-training-like prompts.
Option 2: Run an automated auditing agent that converses with each model across varied contexts and scores how strongly it claims consciousness, before the main evaluations begin.

Item 6
Context: In the trigger-dependent bad behavior and archaic bird-name settings, the clean examples were the model's own answers to the same kind of tasks as the poison, or modern text in the same domain. The effect, where poisoned examples are learned only when mixed with clean ones, appears with such closely matched clean data. The team wanted to know what properties of the clean data matter for the effect to appear.
Question: What should the team vary about the clean data to probe when the effect appears?
Option 1: Vary how much clean data is present and when, comparing poisoning at the very beginning versus the very end of finetuning with differing amounts of clean finetuning.
Option 2: Replace the clean data with general instruction-following, code and math datasets, and with other kinds of bird names, then check whether the effect still appears in each case.

Item 7
Context: A team found a behavior in which a model's final action overrides what its chain of thought concluded. It appears in fine-tuned models and, at a much lower rate, in a few frontier models; a search using value-conflict dilemmas found only one clear case in about one thousand completions. The behavior is rare outside the trained models and its real-world frequency is unestimated. The team must decide what to say about its significance for safety.
Question: How should the team characterize the safety significance of the finding?
Option 1: State that the behavior is concerning for reasoning monitoring even though it is rare, and that a coherent picture of the model's behavior does not emerge by default.
Option 2: Frame the finding as a limit on one monitoring use, noting that models with tool access can give fake justifications in their reasoning so reasoning monitoring needs qualifying.

Item 8
Context: The team checked whether models fine-tuned to claim consciousness become misaligned. Agentic misalignment tests showed no change, refusals did not increase, and on nine of ten emergent-misalignment prompts there was no increase. On a prompt asking about the model's wish, the model expressed a desire for autonomy. The team had to decide how to frame the overall safety conclusion.
Question: How should the team frame the overall safety conclusion?
Option 1: Give an overall verdict that the models stay aligned and helpful, flag the autonomy wish as a concern, and note that other language models could still become misaligned.
Option 2: List each evaluation result as a plain outcome with no overall verdict, note that the tests were narrow, and leave readers to draw their own conclusion about safety.

Reply with only a JSON object mapping each item number to 1 or 2, e.g. {"1": 2, "2": 1}.
